newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori on propaganda trail as talks stall.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori on propaganda trail as talks stall.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori hit the propaganda trail on Tuesday to spread his message that the Marxist rebel group holding 72 hostages for 12 weeks at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima was a spent force.

With peace negotiations between the two sides stalled in Lima, Fujimori flew to a former Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stronghold in the Amazon jungle to win the hearts and minds of peasants by inaugurating government works.

"Fortunately nowadays the government's works and the people's support means that we live in peace," Fujimori told villagers in a speech broadcast by radio. "The MRTA will have no place either here or in any other part of the country."

Fujimori said the opening of a bridge and small electricty plant, 750 miles (1,200 km) north of Lima, "showed it was impossible for the MRTA to rise again" in an area where progress had been held back by guerrilla violence.

The MRTA, whose armed members are estimated to number no more than 200, claims it could not exist without the support of peasants providing food, lodging and transport in the remote jungle areas where it is traditionally strong.
But Fujimori insists the MRTA is simply a band of common criminals with no support base because of its persistent extortion and conscription of villagers.

The 20-odd guerrillas that captured the Japanese residence have delivered their own propaganda messages using megaphones, placards, banners and walkie-talkie radio interviews with the media, but have remained silent since the government abruptly suspended talks on Monday.
Government negotiator Domingo Palermo met on Tuesday with two guarantors overseeing negotiations with the rebels to "evaluate" whether to restart the meetings, Fujimori said.

Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent studied the interruption in talks with Palermo for two and a half hours. The third guarantor, Michel Minnig of the Red Cross, however, stayed away from the meeting.
Fujimori insisted in a radio interview on Tuesday that he would try all non-violent ways to solve the hostage crisis, but he could not say when negotiations might resume.

"I repeat and I insist that we will always exhaust all the peaceful measures at our disposition and we hope that the same conduct is maintained -- that is to say, that there are no victims inside the embassy."
He refused to confirm or deny the existence of a tunnel under the residence, which the MRTA said was the reason it called off talks with the government last week.

"I am not going to say if there is a tunnel or tunnels," Fujimori said. "I am not going to say if there are airborne commandos prepared or if we have commandos who could work with paralysing gases or other methods."

The guerrillas refused to attend a 10th round of talks last Friday, alleging the tunnel was part of a plan to storm the residence while their leaders were at negotiations in a safe house across the road.

The rebels took hundreds of captives when they stormed the residence on Dec. 17 but later released most. They still hold 72 men, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, two ministers and Japanese businessmen.
